title: Cloud Reference Architecture
overview: Use reference architectures to connect business requirements to cloud components. Compare cloud-native and cloud-enabled designs, migration routes, IaC, image security and hybrid or multi-cloud placement. The worked e-commerce, gaming and recovery designs show why each component is needed.
big_ideas: Cloud-native apps are designed for multi-tenancy, elastic scaling and easy integration; cloud-enabled apps are traditional apps moved to the cloud.
Microservices on orchestrated containers are one common cloud-native design; serverless and other styles can also apply cloud principles.
Lift and shift minimises initial change; partial or complete refactoring can improve cloud fit when the gains justify cost and time.
Infrastructure as Code makes environments repeatable, versioned, documented and rebuildable; declarative IaC states the desired end state.
Secure container images are minimal, official, patched, non-root, signed, distroless, immutable and standards-compliant.
Hybrid and multi-cloud are different: hybrid mixes cloud types, multi-cloud mixes providers; containers on Kubernetes make workloads movable.
A reference architecture is a reusable template for a domain; start from vendor catalogues, adapt to the use case.

sections.title: Architect roles and where cloud architects fit
sections.summary: Who designs what in an organisation, and the cloud architect's place among them.

items: **Enterprise architects** → set **technical strategy and direction** across the organisation
**Solution architects** → turn **requirements** into a **reusable solution design**, with **business analysts** and **product owners**
**Application architects** → own the design of **one or more specific applications**
**Information architects** → focus on **users' experience of the data**
**Infrastructure architects** → design **servers, network, storage and facilities**

notes.lead: Owns the cloud strategy and initiatives:
notes.foot: This is the role **you play in the exam**.

items: Gives these roles a **shared modern template** of **layers and components** to **align on**

terms.def: Sets technical strategy and direction across the organisation.
Converts requirements into a reusable solution design.
Owns cloud strategy, migration plans, cloud-native design and governance.

check.q: A company is about to move 40 applications to the cloud and asks whether its existing solution architects can simply take this on. What gap would a cloud architect fill?

items: **Solution architect**: designs a solution for a **given set of requirements**

items.t: **Cloud architect**: owns the **cloud strategy** across them
sub: oversight of **cloud management and governance policies**

items: **Without that role** → **40 separate solution designs** would each make their own cloud choices
a.foot: A **small estate** could combine the roles, but the **strategy and governance** work still has to be owned by someone.

check.q: Users complain that a reporting portal's data is correct but hard to find and interpret, while the DBA says the schema is well normalised. Which architect role should look at this, and why not the other?

items: **Information architect**: focuses on how users **experience and interact with data**
**Data architect**: designs and manages **data structures**, and the schema is already sound
**The problem** is **presentation and navigation** rather than **storage**

sections.title: Cloud-native vs cloud-enabled
sections.summary: What makes an application cloud-native, why organisations go that way, and why they usually start with lift and shift.

items: Lecture emphasis: **elastic, easily integrated** applications using **orchestrated containers** and **microservices**
notes.foot: These are **common mechanisms**, not requirements: they don't exclude **serverless** or a **well-designed monolith**.

items: **Use IaaS and PaaS** to exploit **elasticity** in a **fail-safe** way
**Scale resources up automatically** under **load or failure**

items.t: How well an app fits the cloud depends on reliance on:

notes.h: Lift and shift often starts adoption
items: Moves infrastructure spending toward a **usage-based operating model**
**Predictable unit prices** ≠ **predictable total spend**: **usage and resource sizing** still matter

terms.def: Designed for cloud properties such as elasticity, resilience, automation and easy integration.
Traditional app moved to the cloud largely unchanged.
Move an application to IaaS with minimal change.

check.q: An enterprise with 200 on-premises VMs and a board deadline wants to start its cloud adoption with lift and shift to IaaS. Is that a sound first step, and what should it not assume?

items: Moves infrastructure spend to a **usage-based operating model** quickly
**Don't assume lower or predictable total spend** → predictable **unit prices** still depend on **sizing and usage**

check.q: Two new projects arrive: an IoT telemetry service with unpredictable device growth, and an internal timesheet tool used by 50 staff. Which should be cloud-native and which can simply be cloud-enabled?

sub: needs **automatic scaling** under load or failure

items: **Timesheet tool → cloud-enabled**: **small, steady load**, so moving it **as is** is enough
a.foot: Native design is only worth its cost where **elasticity, statelessness and automation** actually pay off.

check.q: A teammate says 'it isn't cloud-native unless it runs on Kubernetes with microservices.' Do you agree?

items: **Orchestrated containers and microservices** are common ways to build cloud-native apps
**Defining idea**: design for **cloud properties** such as **elasticity, automation and easy integration**
A **serverless app** or a **well-designed monolith** that **scales and recovers automatically** can also qualify

visuals.title: Cloud-enabled vs cloud-native
rows: Originally developed for a traditional data centre, then moved to the cloud
Developed with cloud principles in mind: multi-tenancy, elastic scaling, easy integration and administration
Often orchestrated containers and microservices; functions or other styles can also fit
Lift and shift to IaaS in the first wave (variable resources, hourly opex)
Greenfield design using IaaS and PaaS to exploit elasticity in a failsafe manner

sections.title: Cloud-native building blocks and ecosystem
sections.summary: The dimensions of choice in a cloud-native design and the ecosystem of components that make containers run in production.

notes.lead: Cloud-native is a menu; the architect's job is to pick per requirement.

sub: scale functions, modules, containers or VMs

notes.h: Container ecosystem: more than a runtime
items: **Service mesh** → handles **service-to-service traffic** (load balancing, encryption, retries)
**API gateways** → **route and secure external traffic** into microservices

notes.foot: Cutting across: **security** (keys, encryption), **observability** and a **service mesh**.

terms.def: Layer managing microservice-to-microservice communication (load balancing, encryption, retries).
Automates deployment, scaling and lifecycle of containers (Kubernetes).
Single secure entry point routing external traffic to microservices.
Deliberately injecting failures to test resilience.

check.q: A team has containers running under a container runtime on three VMs and says they are ready for production. What is missing?

sub: **orchestration** for deployment, scaling and failure recovery

items: **If the services need them**: **persistent storage** and **messaging**
**Without orchestration** → a crashed container or failed VM needs **manual recovery**

check.q: A platform has 6 services behind an API gateway. The team wants a service mesh as well. Would you add it now?

items: **Service mesh** → manages internal **east-west** traffic (**load balancing, encryption, retries**); pays off when many services need **uniform inter-service policy**
**With 6 services** → **library-level retries and TLS** may be enough
a.foot: Revisit when the **service count** or the need for **mutual TLS** and **traffic policy** grows.

check.q: Orders must reach billing, shipping and analytics, and billing is sometimes down for maintenance. Synchronous HTTP API calls or event streaming and messaging?

items: Each consumer processes **at its own pace**
**Billing catches up** after maintenance instead of **failing the order**
**Cost**: **eventual consistency** and an **extra platform** to operate
a.foot: Keep a **synchronous API** where the caller needs an **immediate answer**, such as a **price check**.

sections.title: Migration choices, Infrastructure as Code and image security
sections.summary: How to choose a migration approach, why infrastructure should be code, and how to build secure container images.

items: **Lift and shift** → usually **quickest**, but may **retain inefficiencies**
**Complete refactoring** → can improve **performance and operating cost**, but gains must **justify higher implementation cost, time and risk**
Manages **servers, networks and storage** through **machine-readable definition files**
**Infrastructure code** (**Terraform**, **CloudFormation**, **Ansible**) → builds the **environment it runs in**
**Speed and consistency** → consistent **dev, test and prod templates** with **deliberate environment differences**
**Disaster recovery** → **rebuilding infrastructure**, alongside **restored data and dependencies**

notes.foot: **Declarative** IaC states the **desired end state**; tooling decides **how to reach it**.

items: **Immutable releases** → **replace rather than patch**; **restrict runtime writes** where practical

terms.def: Managing infrastructure through versioned, machine-readable code.
Describe the desired end state; tooling works out the steps.
Image with only runtime dependencies, no shell or package manager.
Fixed deployment artifact replaced by a new version rather than patched in place; a read-only runtime filesystem is a separate hardening setting.

check.q: A legacy app costs a lot to run on lifted VMs because it can't scale down at night. Would you do a complete refactor, a partial refactor or stay lifted?

a.lead: **Partial refactor** is the usual first answer.
items: **Target the component that blocks scale-down** → e.g. extract the **stateless web tier** so it can **autoscale**
**Complete refactor**: only if **measured long-term gains** outweigh its higher **cost, time and risk**
**Stay lifted**: fine if the **night-time waste** is smaller than the **refactoring cost**

check.q: After a regional outage, the team rebuilds its whole network and cluster from IaC in another region in 20 minutes, but the app still won't start. What was most likely missing from the DR plan?

items: **Missing**: the **data, secrets and configuration** the app needs were probably not **restored or replicated** to the recovery region

sub: a way to restore **secrets and config** alongside the IaC

check.q: Engineers fix production servers by hand during incidents, and test now behaves differently from production. How does IaC address this, and what discipline does it require?

items: **Environments in versioned, reviewed code** with **deliberate parameter differences**
**Discipline**: **every change**, including **incident fixes**, goes through the **code and the pipeline**
a.foot: Otherwise **drift** returns, and the **next apply** may **overwrite the hand fix**.

check.q: A scan finds a shell and package manager in a production image that runs as root and is patched in place. Which image practices does this break, and what would you change?

sub: rebuild from a **verified minimal or distroless base**
**replace containers** with a new patched image instead of **patching them in place**

items: **Gain** → shrinks the **attack surface** and limits what an attacker can do **after a compromise**

visuals.title: Lift and shift vs refactoring
rows: Only parts of the app modified
Much higher cost; most of the app must change
Typically none of the native features
Potential gains; validate against workload and total cost

sections.title: Hybrid, multi-cloud and reference architectures
sections.summary: How private, hybrid and multi-cloud designs differ and how reference architectures guide design.

notes.lead: Separate infrastructure ownership from network isolation.
items: **Vendor on-premises stacks** and **cross-cloud tools** support these choices
**1.0** → a **cloud broker** spreads **different workloads** across clouds; **each app stays in one cloud**
**2.0** → **containerises workloads on Kubernetes** so they can be **moved or recreated across clouds**
notes.foot: **Images alone do not move** data, **IAM policies**, networks or **proprietary managed-service dependencies**.

notes.lead: A template solution for a domain.

terms.def: Reusable template solution for an architecture in a given domain.
Intermediary distributing workloads across multiple clouds.
NIST cloud reference architecture describing the actors in cloud computing.

check.q: A firm containerised every app and runs them on Kubernetes in two clouds, and now says it can 'move any workload between clouds in an hour'. What has it overlooked?

items: **Containers and Kubernetes definitions** standardise **packaging and orchestration** (**multi-cloud 2.0**)
**Do not move with the image**: **data**, **IAM policies**, **networking** and dependencies on **proprietary managed services**
A workload using one provider's **managed database** still needs its **data migrated** and its **integration rewritten**
a.foot: The claim holds only for **stateless apps** with **portable dependencies**.

check.q: A company uses a broker to place its HR system on one cloud and its analytics on another, and each app stays in its own cloud. Which multi-cloud generation is this, and what does it fail to give?

items: Workloads are **spread across clouds**, but each app is **tied to one provider**
**Fails to give**: **workload portability** → moving an app means **migrating** it
**Multi-cloud 2.0**: **containerises** workloads so they can be **recreated elsewhere**
a.foot: Multi-cloud 2.0 costs running **Kubernetes consistently** in each cloud.

check.q: You must design a cloud platform for a new government agency. Should you start from a vendor's reference architecture or a neutral one such as NIST 500-292?

a.lead: Use a **neutral** one to frame the **actors and building blocks**, then a **vendor's** reference architecture once the provider is chosen.
items: **Neutral (NIST 500-292 or CCRA)** → keeps the design **vendor-neutral** and helps the agency **compare options**
**Vendor reference architectures** → concrete starting points with **proven component combinations**
a.foot: But vendor ones **lean toward that vendor's services**.

visuals.title: Placement and isolation answer different questions
rows: Operate it yourself or contract its operation
Integrate connectivity, identity and data flows
Plan for API, data and operations differences

sections.title: Worked reference architectures and the case for Kubernetes
sections.summary: Four use-case architectures (e-commerce, gaming, big data, disaster recovery) and why cloud native keeps spreading.

notes.h: Match the architecture to the workload
notes.foot: The skill is **explaining why each component exists**, not memorising products.

sub: routes to separate **Product, Payment, Inventory and Cart** services as **functions**

items: **Auto-scaled web and app servers** across **two Availability Zones** behind a **load balancer**
**Primary database** replicates **synchronously** to a **standby in another AZ** → **availability**
**Snapshots copied automatically** to a **second region** → a **function restores a new instance**
notes.foot: **Synchronous standby** covers **AZ failure**; **cross-region snapshots** cover **regional disaster**.

items: **Heavy ops automation** frees developers from **operations drudgery**

terms.def: Isolated data-centre location within a region used for fault tolerance.
Open-source system for running and managing containers; a cloud portability layer.
Network of edge caches delivering content close to users.

check.q: An online game's player count jumps 10 times during weekend events, and a zone outage last month took it offline. What two design features address these problems, and what does each cost?

items.t: **Auto-scaled web and app tiers** → absorb the **event spikes**
sub: **Cost**: needs **stateless servers**, with **sessions** moved to an **in-memory cache**

items.t: **Two Availability Zones** behind a **load balancer** → keeps the game up if one **zone fails**

check.q: The DR design uses a synchronous standby in a second AZ and snapshots copied to another region. A manager asks why both are needed. Explain, including what each one loses.

sub: **Loses**: does nothing if the **whole region** fails
**Loses**: recover only to the **last copied snapshot**
need **time to restore** a new instance

a.foot: Choose **snapshot frequency** against acceptable **data loss**, and **restore capacity** against acceptable **downtime**.

check.q: An e-commerce team must choose between a classic stack (load-balanced, auto-scaled app servers with a shared relational database) and a serverless design with Product, Payment, Inventory and Cart functions behind an API gateway, each with its own store. Traffic is low most of the year with sharp sale peaks. Which fits, and what do you give up?

items: **Functions scale** with the **sale peaks** and **cost little** in quiet months
**Separate stores** → each service **scales and changes independently**
**Give up**: simple **cross-service transactions and joins** → **inventory and payment consistency** now needs **coordination**
a.foot: A **steady, high base load** would favour the **classic stack**.

exam_angles.q: A company runs a 10-year-old monolith on premises. The data-centre contract ends in 6 months, and the checkout module struggles at month-end peaks. Recommend a migration approach, and say what would justify a complete refactor.

a.lead: **Lift and shift to IaaS first**, then **partially refactor** the checkout module.
items: **Lift and shift** → meets the **6-month deadline** with **minimal change**
**Partial refactor** → e.g. extract checkout as a **stateless, autoscaled service**
**Leave the rest** of the monolith alone until **measured benefits** justify more work
**Complete refactor**: justified only if **long-term performance and operating-cost gains** outweigh its higher **cost, time and risk**
a.foot: Note: the **lifted monolith** may **cost more to run** than expected until it is **optimised**.

exam_angles.q: A platform team manages dev, test and prod by hand, and an outage last quarter took 3 days to recover. Justify Infrastructure as Code, explain how you would keep the environments consistent but deliberately different, and say what IaC will not solve.

items: **Shared, versioned IaC modules** with **explicit per-environment parameters** (**sizes, replica counts**) and **separate state**
**Changes go through Git review** and are **applied automatically** → reduces **drift** and **documents** the environment
**IaC will not restore** **data, secrets or application configuration** → DR also needs **backups or replication** and a **tested recovery runbook**

exam_angles.q: A regulated insurer must keep policyholder data on premises, wants elastic capacity for quote calculations, and its CTO also wants a second public cloud 'to avoid lock-in'. Design the strategy and judge the second cloud.

items: **Stateless quote calculation** on **public cloud**, sending **only the data it needs** over a **secured link**
**Second public cloud** only for a **concrete reason**, such as a **lock-in risk** or a **best-of-breed service**
**Containerising on Kubernetes** → workloads **portable** (**multi-cloud 2.0**), but **data, identity and managed-service dependencies** still tie them to a provider
a.foot: Every added environment increases **integration, skills and management cost**.

exam_angles.q: A startup runs 12 containerised microservices and has had two outages: one from a bad manual deployment and one from a retry storm between services. What components would you add to make the platform production-ready, and which outage does each address?

sub: either a **service mesh** or **consistent client libraries** for **retry limits, timeouts and circuit breaking**
at **12 services** a mesh is **defensible** but adds **operating cost**

exam_angles.q: Design the architecture for an online game with spiky weekend traffic, global players downloading large assets, real-time leaderboards, and a target of surviving a full region outage. Explain each component's purpose.

items: **Auto-scaled web and app tiers** across **two AZs** behind a **load balancer** → handle the **spikes** and **zone failure**
**In-memory cache** → holds **sessions and leaderboards** so servers stay **stateless** and **reads are fast**
**Object storage and a CDN** → serve **large assets** close to players
**Replicated database** with a **synchronous standby** → covers **zone failure**
**Region outage** → **copy snapshots to a second region** and **restore them with automation**
a.foot: Accept **data loss back to the last snapshot** and a **restore delay**.
